It's October 2032. Tomorrow the old chestnut trees on Kastanienallee will be cut down. Today the children are collecting the last conkers. Elif, Jakob and Ludwig are standing under the trees.
Mr Lorenz, why do the trees have to be cut down, even though they still have conkers?
Because they're diseased, Elif. The roots are lifting the pavement, so that old people can trip.
But they don't look diseased at all. Are they being cut down anyway?
People don't always look ill when they're ill either. After all, I look like a young man too.
No, Mr Brandt. You look like an old man.
Children always tell the truth. That's why I like talking to them so much.
Elif, we're collecting all the conkers today so that we can plant new trees in spring. After the old ones have been cut down, the young ones come.
And my conker? The one in the flowerpot?
It's already a little tree. It goes into the ground first. As soon as the new stop is finished, we'll plant it right next to it.
How long does it take until it's as big as these?
About eighty years. While it grows, you'll grow up, have children, maybe grandchildren. And one day your grandchildren will collect conkers here.
And you? Will you still be here then?
No, Elif. But it doesn't matter. You don't plant trees for yourself.
“nakh-DEHM / zo-BALT”: stress on the second syllable.
no change: …, denn sie SIND krank.
the verb right after: Deshalb WERDEN sie gefällt.
weil, obwohl, damit, nachdem, wenn, als, dass, ob
the verb at the end: …, weil sie krank SIND.
Trick for the coordinating ones: ADUSO = aber, denn, und, sondern, oder. These don't change anything.

“um … zu” = in order to, when the subject is the same: “Wir sammeln Kastanien, um Bäume zu pflanzen.” “damit” = so that, especially when the subjects are different: “Wir pflanzen Bäume, damit unsere Enkel Schatten haben.”

Bevor die Bäume fallen, sammeln wir.
Während sie wächst, wirst du groß.
Es dauert lange, bis sie groß ist.
After “nachdem” you use the earlier tense: Plusquamperfekt for the past (nachdem sie gesammelt HATTEN, kamen…), Perfekt for the present (nachdem die alten gefällt SIND, kommen…).

indirect questions (Könnten Sie mir sagen, wann…? / ob…)

The workers came on Monday, the eighteenth of October, at seven in the morning, with two lorries, a crane and four chainsaws. But when they got out of their vehicles, they saw something nobody had expected. Under each of the six old chestnut trees stood people. Not to protest. They simply stood there, silent, in jackets and woolly hats, with coffee cups in their hands. Children, parents, old people. Mr Yilmaz in his bus driver's uniform, before he had to leave for the early shift. Mrs Schulze with her walking frame. The young mother with the twins. The man in the wheelchair. They had come to say goodbye.

The evening before, the children from the primary school, Jakob's class and two more, had collected all the conkers still lying under the trees. There were over three thousand. They were now in crates in the gym, sorted by tree, with little labels: tree 1, tree 2, tree 3. Jakob had explained that over the winter the conkers have to lie in damp sand so that they sprout in spring. Kuba had worked out that three thousand conkers could produce about three hundred trees. “Enough for the whole of Prenzlauer Berg,” he had said proudly. Jakob had laughed and said that only six were needed. But they could give the others away.

The foreman, a tall man with a grey moustache and hands like shovels, stopped, puzzled. Then Mrs Krause from the district office came, who had come too, even though she wasn't on duty, and quietly explained to him what was going on. The man nodded slowly. He took off his helmet. “We've got time,” he said to his colleagues. “We'll start at eight. Let the people say goodbye in peace.” And then he took a Thermos flask out of the lorry and sat down with the others under the first chestnut tree.

Ludwig was standing under the third chestnut tree, the one in front of the old stop, with Lena on one side and Elif on the other. He had stopped under this tree for forty-one years. In summer the passengers had waited in its shade; in autumn conkers had fallen on the roof of the tram with a dull thud that he could still hear today. And once, in May 1975, Ingrid had stood under this tree, with a bunch of white chestnut blossoms, and waited for him, because she wanted to tell him she was pregnant. With Thomas.

He told Elif, who listened wide-eyed, and Lena, who had never heard the story. “Your uncle Thomas,” he said to Lena, “was actually announced under this tree. Before he was born, before he had a name. Ingrid handed me a blossom in the cab, and I left it behind the windscreen all day. The passengers wondered why the driver was smiling so much.”

Lena looked at her grandfather as if she were seeing him for the first time. She knew so many stories from him: the tram, the Wall, the Fairy-Tale Fountain, the house. But he had never told this one. “Why are you only telling this now, Grandpa?” she asked quietly. Ludwig shrugged. “Because that tree was still there,” he said. “As long as something is there, you don't talk about it. You think you still have time. Only when it disappears do you realise that otherwise the story disappears too.” Lena took his phone, which he never used, and took a photo of him under the chestnut tree. The last one.

At half past seven two more people arrived whom nobody was expecting: Susanne, on the night train from Hanover, and Mirko, on the first train from Dresden. They hadn't arranged it. They had both read in the paper that the trees would be cut down, and both, without telling the other, had bought a ticket. They met under the fifth chestnut tree, in front of number thirty-one, and laughed because they had both had the same idea. “It was under this tree that I gave you the love letter,” said Mirko. “In September 1989. You didn't read it while I was there. You waited until I'd gone.”
Of course. Because I knew I'd blush. And after I'd read it, I ran up the stairs and locked myself in the bathroom for three hours, so that my mother thought I was ill.

At eight the people slowly stepped aside. The chainsaws started up. It was loud and fast, much faster than everyone had thought. The branches fell, then the crowns, then the trunks, in big round pieces, which the crane lifted into the lorries. Elif held her ears shut and cried, and Ludwig put his hand on her shoulder, and Lena put her hand on his. Nobody spoke. By eleven o'clock there were six round stumps on Kastanienallee, pale and fresh, and everywhere smelt of wood.

When the last trunk was in the lorry, Mrs Krause took a little notebook out of her bag and wrote something in it. Later she told Lena what it was: the date, the time and the names of all the people who had come. “For the archive,” she said. “So that someone in eighty years will know that these trees didn't die alone.”

Then the foreman did something nobody had asked him to. From the trunk of the third chestnut tree, the one in front of the old stop, he cut a thin round slice, as big as a cartwheel, sanded the surface with a small machine and brought it to Ludwig. “For you,” he said. “Mrs Krause told me you used to drive along here. So did my father. With the BVB, in the seventies. Maybe you knew him. Hans Becker.” Ludwig looked at him for a long time. “Hans Becker,” he said. “The one who always came too early. Who cycled to the depot at four every morning, whatever the weather.” The foreman laughed, and his eyes were wet. “That was him.”

The foreman, who now introduced himself as Uwe Becker, stayed another half hour, even though his colleagues were already loading the lorries. He sat down next to Ludwig on the bench in front of the café and let him tell him about his father: how Hans Becker once, in the winter of 1979, stopped the tram in the middle of the route because a puppy was sitting on the rails and wouldn't move, and how he got out and carried the puppy home, three streets further on, while the passengers waited in the tram and nobody complained. “He never told me that,” said Uwe Becker. “He didn't tell much in general.” “The good ones never tell much,” said Ludwig. “That's what the rest of us are for.”

In the evening they laid the slice of wood on the table in Ludwig's flat and everyone counted the annual rings: Ludwig, Lena, Andrei, Elif, Susanne, Mirko, Mara and Jakob, Kuba and Ola. They counted with pencils, ring by ring, from the outside in, and Elif wrote on a slip of paper what had happened in each year. Here, right on the outside, 2032: the residents' meeting. Further in, 1995: Ludwig buys the house. 1989: the Wall falls, Susanne moves away. 1975: Thomas is announced. 1961: the Wall is built. And right in the middle, in the dark heart, a tiny ring. “Nineteen fifty-two,” Elif counted. “Eighty rings.”

Eighty years. The tree is younger than me. It was a little sapling when I was four and stood at this stop with my mother and was allowed to press the bell. We grew old together, it and I. And now I don't walk under it any more, and it isn't there any more.

Elif looked at him for a long time, with the serious look that only eight-year-olds have. Then she got up, went to the window, where the flowerpot she had brought for this evening stood, and put it on the table next to the slice of wood. The little tree in it was now thirty centimetres tall, with five green leaves that gleamed in the lamplight. “This one,” she said, “has only one ring. But it has eighty more ahead of it. And you can watch it grow, Mr Brandt. Every day, from the window. Because it's right next to the new stop. So that you can ride the tram again and see a tree.”

It was very quiet in the room. Then Ludwig said, in a voice that trembled a little: “Elif, one day you'll be a very good teacher.” And Susanne, who had been a teacher for thirty years, nodded and said: “She already is.” The slice of wood hangs today above the tiled stove in the ground-floor flat, with a small plaque that Andrei had engraved in brass: “Kastanienallee, 1952–2032. Eighty rings. And a new one.”
